top_3_developments.headline: U.S.–Iran war escalated with continued U.S.–Israeli airstrikes and Iranian attacks across the Gulf
top_3_developments.summary: U.S. and Israeli forces continued a large-scale air campaign against Iranian military and regime infrastructure, including fresh March 7 strikes on targets in Tehran and Isfahan and the deployment of a third U.S. aircraft carrier to the region.[1] Iran maintained missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases and diplomatic facilities in multiple Gulf states, causing U.S. fatalities and threatening shipping around the Strait of Hormuz while U.S. officials signaled the operation would continue for weeks.[1][2][3]
top_3_developments.source: [1] 2026 Iran war – Wikipedia; [2] ISW Iran Update, March 2–3, 2026; [3] Global News, March 3, 2026 broadcast

top_3_developments.headline: Trump’s UN-mandated Board of Peace advanced Gaza plan implementation into Phase Two
top_3_developments.summary: The Board of Peace, chaired by Donald Trump under UN Security Council Resolution 2803, moved from initial chartering to operational status and advanced Trump’s 20‑point Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict into Phase Two.[1][2] The Board oversaw the creation of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) under Dr. Ali Sha’ath and began coordinating with a High Representative for Gaza and an International Stabilization Force commander, amid criticism over its broad mandate and limited Palestinian representation.[1][2][3]
top_3_developments.source: [1] White House statements on Gaza Plan and Board of Peace; [2] Arab Center DC analysis; [3] Baker Institute brief

top_3_developments.headline: Gulf sovereign wealth funds sustained aggressive 2025–26 deployments while preparing for possible war-driven disruptions
top_3_developments.summary: Major Gulf sovereign wealth funds, led by Saudi Arabia’s PIF and Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and ADIA, continued large-scale capital deployments focused on AI, digital infrastructure, climate assets, and private credit after deploying about $119 billion in 2025.[1][4] As tensions and potential disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz increased, these funds conducted stress tests and signaled readiness to scale back or redirect capital toward domestic priorities if energy flows were seriously constrained, while for now remaining in active deployment mode.[3][5]
top_3_developments.source: [1] Semafor on Gulf SWF 2025 activity; [3] EnterpriseAM, March 6, 2026; [4] MUFG Research citing Global SWF 2026; [5] Global SWF news, Feb–Mar 2026

signal_status.headline: U.S.–Iran war continues with ongoing U.S.-Israeli airstrikes and Iranian retaliation across the Gulf
signal_status.summary: A U.S.–Israeli air campaign against Iranian military and government targets, including Tehran and Isfahan, is ongoing, with strikes reported as recently as March 7 against infrastructure of the Iranian regime.[2] Iran has responded with missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases in Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, causing multiple U.S. fatalities, and is using regional proxies while attempting to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz.[1][2] Both sides are still engaged in active kinetic operations as the U.S. reinforces its regional posture, including the deployment of a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East.[2][3]
sources: [1] AthenaLab, "Update on the U.S. Military Intervention in Iran," March 2, 2026
[3] Institute for the Study of War, "Iran Update Evening Special Report, March 1, 2026"
[4] Broadcast coverage indicating March 7, 2026 Tehran explosions and ongoing strikes

signal_status.headline: Trump’s UN‑mandated Board of Peace is now operational and moving Gaza plan into Phase Two under EO-backed framework
signal_status.summary: The Board of Peace, chaired by Donald Trump and authorized by UN Security Council Resolution 2803, has moved from charter ratification in January 2026 to active implementation of Trump’s 20‑point Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, including the transition to Phase Two and the formation of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) under Dr. Ali Sha’ath.[1][2][3] The White House states the Board is providing strategic oversight, mobilizing international resources, and coordinating with a newly appointed High Representative for Gaza and an International Stabilization Force commander, while analysts note skepticism over its broad mandate, Trump’s personal control, and the absence of Palestinian representation.[1][2] EO 14375 is being referenced domestically as the legal and organizational vehicle for U.S. executive action and funding alignment behind the Board’s operations and the Gaza plan, but no major departures or reversals from the announced structure and mandate have been reported since the January 2026 statements.[1][2][3]
sources: [1] White House statement on President Trump’s Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict and the Board of Peace (January 2026)
[2] Arab Center DC analysis of Trump’s Board of Peace mandate, UNSCR 2803 authorization, and inaugural Board meeting timeline
[3] Baker Institute brief on progression of Trump’s Gaza peace plan from Phase One to Phase Two and linkage to Board of Peace

signal_status.headline: Gulf sovereign wealth funds are actively ramping and reallocating capital, with PIF, Mubadala, and Abu Dhabi funds pushing large 2025–26 deployments while preparing for potential war‑related disruptions.
signal_status.summary: Gulf SWFs collectively deployed about USD 119 billion in 2025, with the ‘Gulf 7’ led by Saudi Arabia’s PIF and Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala shifting from sheer balance‑sheet expansion toward more strategic, mega‑deal investments in AI, digital infrastructure, climate assets, and private credit.[4][1] PIF was the largest sovereign investor in the US in 2025, including a USD 29 billion acquisition of Electronic Arts, while Mubadala invested roughly USD 24 billion and continues an aggressive global expansion.[1][4] As regional tensions and possible disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz rise, Abu Dhabi and other Gulf funds are actively stress‑testing and refining 2026–2030 strategies, signaling they could temporarily scale back or redirect capital toward national priorities if energy flows are seriously constrained, but currently remain in deployment mode.[3][5]
sources: [1] Semafor, 'Gulf sovereign funds ramp up US bets', Jan 2026 – details on 2025 US deployments, PIF’s EA acquisition, Mubadala’s US$24bn, and Paramount/Warner bid backing.
[4] MUFG Research, 'Middle East Daily', 5 Jan 2026 – Global SWF 2026 Annual Report data on Gulf 7 investing US$119bn in 2025 and shifting from scale to strategy.
[3] EnterpriseAM, 6 Mar 2026 – note on Abu Dhabi SWFs’ potential strategy repurposing and scaling back in case of prolonged Strait of Hormuz disruption; PIF 2026–2030 refocus and capex trimming.
[5] Global SWF news, 26 Feb & 4 Mar 2026 – updates on Gulf SWFs repositioning into private credit and analysis of Hormuz‑related geopolitical stress on SWF strategies.
[2] Alhurra, 9 Feb 2026 – coverage of broader Gulf SWF restructuring, fund mergers, and portfolio reorganization across Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Qatar.

signal_status.headline: DOJ Epstein files remain in flux as public document trove is updated, culled, and partially restored
signal_status.summary: The Department of Justice currently hosts the Epstein Library under the Epstein Files Transparency Act and is actively updating it, with the site marked as last updated on March 7, 2026 and explicitly stating it will be revised as additional documents are identified for release.[3] A CBS News analysis found that, after a January 30, 2026 tranche of more than three million pages, the public collection has since shrunk by over 47,000 files (about 65,500 pages) as DOJ removes and in some cases restores materials, citing protection of survivors and ongoing investigations while lawmakers and survivors criticize perceived over‑redaction and takedowns.[1][2] The broader political and legal fallout remains ongoing, including new document-driven developments in early 2026 and continuing congressional oversight over DOJ’s handling of the releases.[1][2][3]

signal_status.headline: Russia‑Ukraine peace talks remain stalled as early‑March Abu Dhabi round is in doubt and Moscow links progress to Ukrainian territorial concessions
signal_status.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he expected a new round of U.S.-brokered trilateral peace talks with Russia to take place in early March in Abu Dhabi, aimed at finalizing security guarantees and preparing a leadership‑level meeting with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump.[2][3] However, Russian officials are signaling there is little point in continuing talks unless Ukraine agrees to withdraw from Donetsk, and reporting indicates the planned Abu Dhabi round for March 5–6 is uncertain, with political negotiations described as "stuck" despite some technical progress on ceasefire mechanisms and prisoner exchanges.[1][3] On the ground, fighting continues and Ukrainian officials warn of a possible new Russian offensive in Donbas, underscoring that no ceasefire or territorial agreement has been reached yet.[3][4][5]
sources: [1] The Japan Times – Russia weighs halt to peace talks unless Ukraine cedes territory
[2] The Moscow Times – Zelensky says next round of peace talks with Russia expected in March in Abu Dhabi
[3] Wikipedia – 2026 United States–Ukraine–Russia meetings in Geneva (talks outcomes and Abu Dhabi scheduling doubts)
[4] War & Politics 24 (YouTube) – Zelensky video address from Donetsk region on anticipated Russian offensive
[5] Kyiv Post – Ukraine Gains Ground as Drone Threats and Peace Talks Stall
